news.content_title: STAT3 Gene Variant Linked to Liver Cancer in Iraqi Hepatitis B Patients
news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 27, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health STAT3 Gene Variant Linked to Liver Cancer in Iraqi Hepatitis B Patients by November 23, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 STAT3 Gene Variant Linked to Liver Cancer in Iraqi Hepatitis B Patients Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A hospital-based case-control investigation conducted in Iraq has demonstrated a strong statistical association between a specific genetic variation in the STAT3 gene and an increased risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma among patients infected with the hepatitis B virus. Hepatocellular carcinoma, recognized globally as the sixth most common cancer and the third leading cause of cancer-related mortality, frequently arises in the context of persistent viral hepatitis infections. While global vaccination efforts have targeted the spread of hepatitis B virus, chronic infection remains a notable public health concern in Iraq. Because progression from chronic hepatitis B to primary liver malignancy involves a complex interplay between viral factors, environmental influences, and host genetic susceptibility, researchers sought to clarify the specific contribution of host genomic architecture within this population. The investigation specifically targeted the rs1053004 single-nucleotide polymorphism located within the 3-prime untranslated region of the STAT3 gene, evaluating its potential utility as a predictive molecular marker for liver cancer among Iraqi patients suffering from chronic hepatitis B infection. The study was designed and conducted at Al-Hussaini Teaching Hospital situated in Karbala, Iraq, enrolling participants between December 2024 and June 2025 following formal ethical clearance from the Research Management Unit of the Karbala Health Directorate. To evaluate disease susceptibility systematically, the clinical investigation enrolled 240 individuals categorized into three equal, mutually exclusive cohorts of 80 participants each. The primary clinical group consisted of 80 patients diagnosed with hepatocellular carcinoma arising on a background of chronic hepatitis B infection. The second cohort comprised 80 patients diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B without clinical evidence of malignancy, defined by persistent hepatitis B surface antigen positivity exceeding six months alongside elevated alanine aminotransferase concentrations. The third cohort served as a normal control group consisting of 80 healthy individuals exhibiting normal liver function profiles and confirmed negative serology for both hepatitis B and hepatitis C viruses. Stringent exclusion criteria were applied across all cohorts to exclude confounding liver etiologies, eliminating individuals presenting with autoimmune liver disease, alcoholic liver disease, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson’s disease, human immunodeficiency virus or hepatitis C virus coinfections, or any prior history of other malignancies. Diagnostic confirmation of hepatocellular carcinoma relied primarily on dynamic radiological imaging adhering strictly to the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases criteria. All suspected patients underwent multiphasic contrast-enhanced computed tomography, dynamic magnetic resonance imaging, or both modalities, with diagnosis established by the presence of pathognomonic vascular hallmarks consisting of arterial phase hyperenhancement followed by washout during subsequent portal venous or delayed phases. Through this rigorous radiological assessment, 71 patients had hepatocellular carcinoma confirmed exclusively by noninvasive vascular imaging findings, while nine individuals presenting with atypical imaging characteristics required formal histopathological verification. Serum alpha-fetoprotein concentrations were collected as supportive clinical data rather than an isolated diagnostic standard, ensuring regenerative and dysplastic nodules were accurately distinguished from true neoplastic lesions. Discover more Cancer Find Cancer Care cancer Study Biology Order DNA Kits Baseline demographic and clinical profiling revealed notable divergences among the three study cohorts, underscoring typical patterns of chronic liver disease progression. The mean age was significantly higher in the liver cancer cohort at 59.7 years compared to 48.2 years in the chronic hepatitis B group and 45.6 years in the healthy control group. Male participants constituted a majority across all categories, but the male-to-female ratio peaked markedly within the hepatocellular carcinoma cohort at 2.8 to 1, contrasting with 1.9 to 1 in the chronic hepatitis group and 1.5 to 1 in the healthy controls. Liver cirrhosis was substantially more prevalent among cancer patients, identified in 78.8 percent of the malignant cohort compared to 32.5 percent of the chronic hepatitis group. Furthermore, median serum alpha-fetoprotein reached 328.5 nanograms per milliliter in the cancer group, compared with 6.2 nanograms per milliliter in chronic carriers and 3.4 nanograms per milliliter in controls. Circulating median viral load was also distinctly elevated in malignant cases at 4.7 times 10 to the fifth international units per milliliter compared to 2.3 times 10 to the fourth in chronic carriers, alongside significant alterations in bilirubin, albumin, aspartate aminotransferase, and alanine aminotransferase levels. To obtain reliable molecular profiles, genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood leukocytes using commercial silica-membrane mini spin columns, with nucleic acid purity verified spectrophotometrically by maintaining absorbance ratios between 1.8 and 2.0. Genotyping of the STAT3 rs1053004 locus was performed using a standardized TaqMan allelic discrimination assay utilizing real-time polymerase chain reaction thermal cycling parameters consisting of initial denaturation at 95 degrees Celsius followed by 40 cycles of denaturation and combined annealing-extension at 60 degrees Celsius. To ensure analytical accuracy and validate assay reliability, approximately ten percent of randomly selected samples were independently regenotyped using tetra-primer allele-specific amplification, also known as ARMS-PCR, with sequence-specific oligonucleotides targeting the respective T and C alleles alongside an internal positive control amplicon. Cross-platform validation demonstrated one hundred percent concordance between the fluorescent probe assay and gel-resolved allele-specific amplification, while genotype distributions in the healthy control population conformed to Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium expectations. Analysis of genotype frequencies demonstrated significant differences across the clinical cohorts. Within the hepatocellular carcinoma cohort, the homozygous TT genotype accounted for 48.8 percent, the heterozygous CT genotype represented 38.8 percent, and the homozygous ancestral CC genotype constituted 12.4 percent. In contrast, the chronic hepatitis B cohort exhibited 35.0 percent TT, 45.0 percent CT, and 20.0 percent CC, while the healthy control cohort displayed 25.0 percent TT, 47.5 percent CT, and 27.5 percent CC. Allelic distribution mirrored this progressive variation, as the frequency of the T allele was calculated at 68.1 percent in liver cancer cases, 57.5 percent in chronic hepatitis patients, and 48.8 percent in healthy controls, yielding a crude allelic odds ratio of 2.24 when comparing cancer patients directly against healthy controls. Multivariate logistic regression modeling adjusted for key potential confounding variables, including participant age, biological sex, smoking history, and the presence of underlying liver cirrhosis. Under a codominant inheritance framework comparing cancer patients with healthy controls, individuals harboring the homozygous TT genotype exhibited a statistically significant 4.26-fold increase in the adjusted odds of developing hepatocellular carcinoma relative to those carrying the homozygous CC reference genotype. Although carriers of the heterozygous CT genotype displayed a trend toward higher disease odds relative to CC, this did not reach independent statistical significance. Under a dominant genetic model combining TT and CT genotypes against CC carriers, the presence of the T allele yielded an adjusted odds ratio of 2.72. When comparing hepatocellular carcinoma patients directly to chronic hepatitis B carriers, the homozygous TT genotype remained a statistically significant risk factor under the codominant model, yielding an adjusted odds ratio of 2.18, as well as under the recessive model with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.85. Stratified clinical analyses further clarified how specific viral and host physiological environments modulate the magnitude of this genetic risk. When evaluating TT carriers versus combined CT and CC carriers across clinical subgroups, the association with liver cancer was notably magnified among individuals testing negative for the hepatitis B e antigen, yielding an adjusted odds ratio of 2.86 compared to 1.52 in antigen-positive individuals. A pronounced divergence was also documented based on viral replication intensity: participants presenting with high circulating viral loads of at least 100,000 international units per milliliter exhibited an adjusted odds ratio of 3.14, whereas those with lower viral titers showed an odds ratio of 1.68 that lacked statistical significance. Similarly, among patients with documented liver cirrhosis, the presence of the TT genotype conferred an adjusted odds ratio of 2.97 compared to 1.43 in non-cirrhotic subjects, pointing to meaningful biological interactions between host genotype, prolonged viral replication, and extensive chronic hepatic parenchymal remodeling. Within the hepatocellular carcinoma patient cohort, the STAT3 rs1053004 genotype exhibited distinct correlations with markers of tumor aggressiveness and clinical staging. Patients carrying the TT genotype presented with significantly higher median serum alpha-fetoprotein levels of 512.6 nanograms per milliliter, compared to 285.3 in CT carriers and 147.8 in CC homozygotes. Median circulating viral loads were likewise significantly higher in TT carriers at 8.3 times 10 to the fifth international units per milliliter relative to 3.6 times 10 to the fifth in CT patients and 1.9 times 10 to the fifth in CC patients. Furthermore, 56.4 percent of TT homozygotes were diagnosed with advanced Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer stages C or D, compared to 38.7 percent of CT carriers and 30.0 percent of CC carriers. In contrast, no statistically significant associations emerged between rs1053004 genotypes and gross anatomical tumor diameter, single versus multifocal tumor count, microscopic vascular invasion, or Child-Pugh liver functional grading. The biological rationale connecting this specific genetic polymorphism to oncogenesis centers on the regulatory function of the STAT3 signaling pathway in hepatocarcinogenesis. STAT3 serves as a pivotal downstream transcription factor in the JAK/STAT signaling cascade, governing critical cellular programs including tumor cell proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, and resistance to immune-mediated destruction. Because the rs1053004 single-nucleotide variant is situated in the 3-prime untranslated region of the STAT3 gene, functional annotations from genomic databases indicate its presence in a functional regulatory zone supported by chromatin accessibility, transcription factor binding assays, and expression quantitative trait loci. Genetic alterations in this untranslated domain can disrupt microRNA binding sites and posttranscriptional regulatory mechanisms, potentially leading to dysregulated STAT3 expression and enhanced oncogenic signaling during persistent viral infection. Despite these robust statistical findings, the investigators highlighted several essential methodological limitations that require cautious interpretation. Because the study was conducted within a single medical center with a relatively modest sample size of 240 participants, generalizability remains circumscribed and certain subgroup comparisons lost statistical significance following corrections for multiple hypothesis testing. Additionally, the analysis was restricted to a single locus rather than comprehensive STAT3 haplotype blocks, and direct functional experiments evaluating gene transcription within patient hepatocytes were not performed. The researchers noted that while multivariate models adjusted for underlying cirrhosis, the profound disparity in cirrhosis prevalence between cancer and hepatitis cohorts suggests residual confounding could persist. Consequently, larger multicenter investigations across diverse cohorts and functional cellular assays will be required to validate these findings and determine whether integrating STAT3 genotyping into clinical stratification algorithms can improve early detection of hepatocellular carcinoma in high-risk patients with chronic hepatitis B. Hepatocellular carcinoma, recognized globally as the sixth most common cancer and the third leading cause of cancer-related mortality, frequently arises in the context of persistent viral hepatitis infections. While global vaccination efforts have targeted the spread of hepatitis B virus, chronic infection remains a notable public health concern in Iraq. Because progression from chronic hepatitis B to primary liver malignancy involves a complex interplay between viral factors, environmental influences, and host genetic susceptibility, researchers sought to clarify the specific contribution of host genomic architecture within this population. The investigation specifically targeted the rs1053004 single-nucleotide polymorphism located within the 3-prime untranslated region of the STAT3 gene, evaluating its potential utility as a predictive molecular marker for liver cancer among Iraqi patients suffering from chronic hepatitis B infection. The study was designed and conducted at Al-Hussaini Teaching Hospital situated in Karbala, Iraq, enrolling participants between December 2024 and June 2025 following formal ethical clearance from the Research Management Unit of the Karbala Health Directorate. To evaluate disease susceptibility systematically, the clinical investigation enrolled 240 individuals categorized into three equal, mutually exclusive cohorts of 80 participants each. The primary clinical group consisted of 80 patients diagnosed with hepatocellular carcinoma arising on a background of chronic hepatitis B infection. The second cohort comprised 80 patients diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B without clinical evidence of malignancy, defined by persistent hepatitis B surface antigen positivity exceeding six months alongside elevated alanine aminotransferase concentrations. The third cohort served as a normal control group consisting of 80 healthy individuals exhibiting normal liver function profiles and confirmed negative serology for both hepatitis B and hepatitis C viruses. Stringent exclusion criteria were applied across all cohorts to exclude confounding liver etiologies, eliminating individuals presenting with autoimmune liver disease, alcoholic liver disease, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson’s disease, human immunodeficiency virus or hepatitis C virus coinfections, or any prior history of other malignancies. Diagnostic confirmation of hepatocellular carcinoma relied primarily on dynamic radiological imaging adhering strictly to the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases criteria. All suspected patients underwent multiphasic contrast-enhanced computed tomography, dynamic magnetic resonance imaging, or both modalities, with diagnosis established by the presence of pathognomonic vascular hallmarks consisting of arterial phase hyperenhancement followed by washout during subsequent portal venous or delayed phases. Through this rigorous radiological assessment, 71 patients had hepatocellular carcinoma confirmed exclusively by noninvasive vascular imaging findings, while nine individuals presenting with atypical imaging characteristics required formal histopathological verification. Serum alpha-fetoprotein concentrations were collected as supportive clinical data rather than an isolated diagnostic standard, ensuring regenerative and dysplastic nodules were accurately distinguished from true neoplastic lesions. Discover more Cancer Find Cancer Care cancer Study Biology Order DNA Kits Baseline demographic and clinical profiling revealed notable divergences among the three study cohorts, underscoring typical patterns of chronic liver disease progression. The mean age was significantly higher in the liver cancer cohort at 59.7 years compared to 48.2 years in the chronic hepatitis B group and 45.6 years in the healthy control group. Male participants constituted a majority across all categories, but the male-to-female ratio peaked markedly within the hepatocellular carcinoma cohort at 2.8 to 1, contrasting with 1.9 to 1 in the chronic hepatitis group and 1.5 to 1 in the healthy controls. Liver cirrhosis was substantially more prevalent among cancer patients, identified in 78.8 percent of the malignant cohort compared to 32.5 percent of the chronic hepatitis group. Furthermore, median serum alpha-fetoprotein reached 328.5 nanograms per milliliter in the cancer group, compared with 6.2 nanograms per milliliter in chronic carriers and 3.4 nanograms per milliliter in controls. Circulating median viral load was also distinctly elevated in malignant cases at 4.7 times 10 to the fifth international units per milliliter compared to 2.3 times 10 to the fourth in chronic carriers, alongside significant alterations in bilirubin, albumin, aspartate aminotransferase, and alanine aminotransferase levels. To obtain reliable molecular profiles, genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood leukocytes using commercial silica-membrane mini spin columns, with nucleic acid purity verified spectrophotometrically by maintaining absorbance ratios between 1.8 and 2.0. Genotyping of the STAT3 rs1053004 locus was performed using a standardized TaqMan allelic discrimination assay utilizing real-time polymerase chain reaction thermal cycling parameters consisting of initial denaturation at 95 degrees Celsius followed by 40 cycles of denaturation and combined annealing-extension at 60 degrees Celsius. To ensure analytical accuracy and validate assay reliability, approximately ten percent of randomly selected samples were independently regenotyped using tetra-primer allele-specific amplification, also known as ARMS-PCR, with sequence-specific oligonucleotides targeting the respective T and C alleles alongside an internal positive control amplicon. Cross-platform validation demonstrated one hundred percent concordance between the fluorescent probe assay and gel-resolved allele-specific amplification, while genotype distributions in the healthy control population conformed to Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium expectations. Analysis of genotype frequencies demonstrated significant differences across the clinical cohorts. Within the hepatocellular carcinoma cohort, the homozygous TT genotype accounted for 48.8 percent, the heterozygous CT genotype represented 38.8 percent, and the homozygous ancestral CC genotype constituted 12.4 percent. In contrast, the chronic hepatitis B cohort exhibited 35.0 percent TT, 45.0 percent CT, and 20.0 percent CC, while the healthy control cohort displayed 25.0 percent TT, 47.5 percent CT, and 27.5 percent CC. Allelic distribution mirrored this progressive variation, as the frequency of the T allele was calculated at 68.1 percent in liver cancer cases, 57.5 percent in chronic hepatitis patients, and 48.8 percent in healthy controls, yielding a crude allelic odds ratio of 2.24 when comparing cancer patients directly against healthy controls. Multivariate logistic regression modeling adjusted for key potential confounding variables, including participant age, biological sex, smoking history, and the presence of underlying liver cirrhosis. Under a codominant inheritance framework comparing cancer patients with healthy controls, individuals harboring the homozygous TT genotype exhibited a statistically significant 4.26-fold increase in the adjusted odds of developing hepatocellular carcinoma relative to those carrying the homozygous CC reference genotype. Although carriers of the heterozygous CT genotype displayed a trend toward higher disease odds relative to CC, this did not reach independent statistical significance. Under a dominant genetic model combining TT and CT genotypes against CC carriers, the presence of the T allele yielded an adjusted odds ratio of 2.72. When comparing hepatocellular carcinoma patients directly to chronic hepatitis B carriers, the homozygous TT genotype remained a statistically significant risk factor under the codominant model, yielding an adjusted odds ratio of 2.18, as well as under the recessive model with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.85. Stratified clinical analyses further clarified how specific viral and host physiological environments modulate the magnitude of this genetic risk. When evaluating TT carriers versus combined CT and CC carriers across clinical subgroups, the association with liver cancer was notably magnified among individuals testing negative for the hepatitis B e antigen, yielding an adjusted odds ratio of 2.86 compared to 1.52 in antigen-positive individuals. A pronounced divergence was also documented based on viral replication intensity: participants presenting with high circulating viral loads of at least 100,000 international units per milliliter exhibited an adjusted odds ratio of 3.14, whereas those with lower viral titers showed an odds ratio of 1.68 that lacked statistical significance. Similarly, among patients with documented liver cirrhosis, the presence of the TT genotype conferred an adjusted odds ratio of 2.97 compared to 1.43 in non-cirrhotic subjects, pointing to meaningful biological interactions between host genotype, prolonged viral replication, and extensive chronic hepatic parenchymal remodeling. Within the hepatocellular carcinoma patient cohort, the STAT3 rs1053004 genotype exhibited distinct correlations with markers of tumor aggressiveness and clinical staging. Patients carrying the TT genotype presented with significantly higher median serum alpha-fetoprotein levels of 512.6 nanograms per milliliter, compared to 285.3 in CT carriers and 147.8 in CC homozygotes. Median circulating viral loads were likewise significantly higher in TT carriers at 8.3 times 10 to the fifth international units per milliliter relative to 3.6 times 10 to the fifth in CT patients and 1.9 times 10 to the fifth in CC patients. Furthermore, 56.4 percent of TT homozygotes were diagnosed with advanced Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer stages C or D, compared to 38.7 percent of CT carriers and 30.0 percent of CC carriers. In contrast, no statistically significant associations emerged between rs1053004 genotypes and gross anatomical tumor diameter, single versus multifocal tumor count, microscopic vascular invasion, or Child-Pugh liver functional grading. The biological rationale connecting this specific genetic polymorphism to oncogenesis centers on the regulatory function of the STAT3 signaling pathway in hepatocarcinogenesis. STAT3 serves as a pivotal downstream transcription factor in the JAK/STAT signaling cascade, governing critical cellular programs including tumor cell proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, and resistance to immune-mediated destruction. Because the rs1053004 single-nucleotide variant is situated in the 3-prime untranslated region of the STAT3 gene, functional annotations from genomic databases indicate its presence in a functional regulatory zone supported by chromatin accessibility, transcription factor binding assays, and expression quantitative trait loci. Genetic alterations in this untranslated domain can disrupt microRNA binding sites and posttranscriptional regulatory mechanisms, potentially leading to dysregulated STAT3 expression and enhanced oncogenic signaling during persistent viral infection. Despite these robust statistical findings, the investigators highlighted several essential methodological limitations that require cautious interpretation. Because the study was conducted within a single medical center with a relatively modest sample size of 240 participants, generalizability remains circumscribed and certain subgroup comparisons lost statistical significance following corrections for multiple hypothesis testing. Additionally, the analysis was restricted to a single locus rather than comprehensive STAT3 haplotype blocks, and direct functional experiments evaluating gene transcription within patient hepatocytes were not performed. The researchers noted that while multivariate models adjusted for underlying cirrhosis, the profound disparity in cirrhosis prevalence between cancer and hepatitis cohorts suggests residual confounding could persist. Consequently, larger multicenter investigations across diverse cohorts and functional cellular assays will be required to validate these findings and determine whether integrating STAT3 genotyping into clinical stratification algorithms can improve early detection of hepatocellular carcinoma in high-risk patients with chronic hepatitis B. news.content: Advanced Search Home News Releases Multimedia Meetings Login Register News Release 23-Nov-2026 Mass cytometry reveals cell type-specific immune remodeling in placentas of women with chronic hepatitis B infection Peer-Reviewed Publication Xia & He Publishing Inc. Facebook X LinkedIn WeChat Bluesky Message WhatsApp Email image: These exploratory findings suggest that HBV may reshape placental immunity through enhanced NK cell activation, broad basophil suppression, and disrupted marker coordination. The sample size was limited (n = 20), so the results need to be validated in larger cohorts. These findings provide new perspectives for understanding the mechanisms of mother-to-child transmission. view more Credit: Junfeng Lu, Yunxia Zhu Background and Aims Hepatitis B virus (HBV) vertical transmission remains a major health challenge, and the characteristics of the placental immune microenvironment in chronic infection remain unclear. This study aimed to use mass cytometry to comprehensively analyze phenotypic changes in placental immune cell subsets. Methods We collected placental tissues from 20 pregnant women (6 healthy controls and 14 with chronic HBV infection). CD45+ leukocytes were detected using a 35-marker antibody panel. Unsupervised clustering identified 14 clusters, of which 13 immune clusters were analyzed. Results HBV mainly caused functional remodeling of placental immune cells rather than changes in cell composition (P > 0.05 for all subsets). In natural killer (NK) cells, CD38 (P = 0.015) and CD16 (P = 0.0020) were notably upregulated and strongly correlated (ρ = 0.872, P < 0.001), suggesting potentially enhanced antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) function. T cells showed upregulation of CD27, CD38, and CXCR5. Basophils exhibited the most pronounced changes: 9 differential markers (including chemokine receptors CCR4 and CCR7) were consistently downregulated. Classical monocytes showed an M1 polarization tendency (CD38↑, CD163↓). All P-values were raw; no markers remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction at an FDR threshold of < 0.1, indicating nominal significance. In addition, the coordinated expression patterns of markers within multiple cell subsets were weakened after infection. Conclusions In summary, this study reveals that HBV infection induces functional remodeling rather than compositional changes in placental immune cells. NK cells and T cells showed upregulation of activation and cytotoxicity markers, suggesting enhanced ADCC function; however, basophils showed extensive downregulation of migration-related markers and loss of expression coordination—an unprecedented finding. The weakening of coordination between multiple marker pairs suggests that HBV infection has disrupted the immune regulatory network. To our knowledge, this study is the first to apply high-dimensional single-cell technology to comprehensively characterize the immune-cell landscape in sampled placental tissue, identify the novel phenomenon of basophil functional downregulation, and introduce marker coordination analysis as a methodological approach. These findings provide new insights into the immunological mechanisms underlying HBV MTCT. Future studies should prioritize functional validation of basophil changes (IL-4/IL-13 secretion) and their association with transmission outcomes, as well as verification in larger-scale longitudinal cohorts. In particular, a prospective cohort with documented MTCT outcomes and paired neonatal blood samples is needed to determine whether the placental immune signatures identified here correlate with HBV-specific T-cell responses in neonates. The candidate markers identified in this study provide a basis for subsequent mechanistic research and clinical translation. Kennedy Jr. last year By John Johnson withNewser.AI Posted Nov 24, 2026 12:25 PM CST Copied (Getty/Sementsova Lesia) Fewer US newborns are leaving the hospital with a hepatitis B shot in their system. A new analysis of 1.3 million births finds that 65.6% of babies received the vaccine within 24 hours in early 2026, down from about 80% between 2020 and 2022, reports the Wall Street Journal. The data is published in the New England Journal of Medicine. The decline accelerated after a federal advisory panel in late 2025 scrapped its long-standing recommendation that every newborn get the first dose, instead telling parents of babies born to hepatitis B-negative mothers to consult their doctors. The panel's members were hand-picked by Secretary of Health Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine skeptic, notes the Washington Post. "The bottom line is confusion creates inaction among parents," says Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, an author of the study and a former leader at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "It's as clear as mud what to do because you have public messaging that sheds doubt on the effectiveness of the hepatitis B vaccine." Though the federal policy shift is tied up in court and the shot is still recommended for infants of infected mothers, vaccination rates fell for those high-risk babies, too, from as high as 98% to 93.9%. Since the vaccine became available in the 1980s, the number of early childhood infections has fallen from more than 25,000 annually to fewer than 100. news.title_original: Newborn Hepatitis B Vaccinations See Sharp Drop - Newser

analysis.time: The decline in newborn hepatitis B vaccinations accelerated after a federal advisory panel in late 2025 scrapped its long-standing recommendation, and the data is published in the New England Journal of Medicine.
analysis.location_and_population: The issue is reported in the United States, focusing on newborns, particularly those born to hepatitis B-negative mothers.
analysis.event: Newborn hepatitis B vaccination rates have sharply declined, with 65.6% of babies receiving the vaccine within 24 hours in early 2026, down from about 80% between 2020 and 2022. This decline is linked to a federal advisory panel's decision to change its recommendation.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: A new analysis of 1.3 million births found a significant drop in vaccination rates, with high-risk babies (infants of infected mothers) seeing a decrease from 98% to 93.9%. The decline may threaten progress in reducing early childhood infections, which had fallen from over 25,000 annually to fewer than 100 since the vaccine became available in the 1980s.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The federal policy shift is tied up in court, and the shot is still recommended for infants of infected mothers. However, the decline in vaccination rates has raised concerns about potential reversal of progress in preventing hepatitis B infections.

analysis.brief_en: Newborn hepatitis B vaccination rates in the United States have sharply declined, according to a new analysis of 1.3 million births. In early 2026, only 65.6% of babies received the vaccine within 24 hours, down from about 80% between 2020 and 2022. This drop follows a federal advisory panel's decision in late 2025 to remove its long-standing recommendation for universal vaccination, instead advising parents of babies born to hepatitis B-negative mothers to consult their doctors. The change has led to confusion among parents, as noted by Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, an author of the study and former CDC leader. Despite the policy shift being in court, vaccination rates for high-risk infants (those born to infected mothers) also fell, from 98% to 93.9%. Since the vaccine became available in the 1980s, early childhood hepatitis B infections have dropped from over 25,000 annually to fewer than 100. However, a separate analysis warns that this progress may be reversed if vaccination rates continue to decline. The New England Journal of Medicine published the data, highlighting the potential public health risk.

The company noted that China's National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) has approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) in combination with nucleos(t)ide analogue (NAs) therapy to achieve functional cure of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in non-cirrhotic adult patients. These patients are currently on NAs for at least 6 months, and have HBV DNA <90 IU/mL and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels =3,000 IU/mL. The approval is based on phase III data demonstrating unprecedented functional cure rates compared to standard of care. Bepirovirsen is a first-in-class antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) and offers unprecedented functional cure rates compared to current standard of care alone, and the safety profile is generally well tolerated. The approval was granted under Breakthrough Therapy and Priority Review designations, recognising the high unmet need in China and potential for substantial clinical improvement over existing therapies. GSK said it is collaborating with SBP Group, through its subsidiary Chia Tai Tianqing Pharmaceutical Group Co., Ltd., to accelerate the launch and access of Hibsago in mainland China. Tony Wood, Chief Scientific Officer, GSK, said: "Chronic hepatitis B affects an estimated 75 million people in China. Despite a strong focus on diagnosis and access to treatment, many patients face a lifetime of therapy and remain at risk of long-term liver complications with current standard of care. The accelerated approval of Hibsago means eligible patients in China now have the potential to achieve functional cure with a six-month treatment course." According to the company, CHB is a national health priority in China. The Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Viral Hepatitis (2025-2030) in the country aims for at least 80 percent of people living with CHB to be diagnosed, and at least 80 percent of newly reported patients treated by 2030. In London, GSK shares were trading at 1,930.68 pence, up 0.58 percent. The company noted that China's National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) has approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) in combination with nucleos(t)ide analogue (NAs) therapy to achieve functional cure of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in non-cirrhotic adult patients. These patients are currently on NAs for at least 6 months, and have HBV DNA <90 IU/mL and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels =3,000 IU/mL. The approval is based on phase III data demonstrating unprecedented functional cure rates compared to standard of care. Bepirovirsen is a first-in-class antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) and offers unprecedented functional cure rates compared to current standard of care alone, and the safety profile is generally well tolerated. The approval was granted under Breakthrough Therapy and Priority Review designations, recognising the high unmet need in China and potential for substantial clinical improvement over existing therapies. GSK said it is collaborating with SBP Group, through its subsidiary Chia Tai Tianqing Pharmaceutical Group Co., Ltd., to accelerate the launch and access of Hibsago in mainland China. Tony Wood, Chief Scientific Officer, GSK, said: "Chronic hepatitis B affects an estimated 75 million people in China. Despite a strong focus on diagnosis and access to treatment, many patients face a lifetime of therapy and remain at risk of long-term liver complications with current standard of care. The accelerated approval of Hibsago means eligible patients in China now have the potential to achieve functional cure with a six-month treatment course." According to the company, CHB is a national health priority in China. The Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Viral Hepatitis (2025-2030) in the country aims for at least 80 percent of people living with CHB to be diagnosed, and at least 80 percent of newly reported patients treated by 2030. In London, GSK shares were trading at 1,930.68 pence, up 0.58 percent. Precision BioSciences (NASDAQ:DTIL) plans to advance its hepatitis B gene-editing treatment into a Phase II study and expects initial biopsy results from its Duchenne muscular dystrophy program in 2027, executives said at a Jefferies conference. Chief Scientific Officer Cassie Gorsuch said the hepatitis B study will test whether the company's treatment, PBGENE-HBV, can reduce enough of the viral material known as cccDNA to achieve a viral cure. Chief Operating Officer Alex Kelly said the company expects to begin seeing Phase II data in the second half of 2027. → Gold Is Down 35%—Is the Bull Case Broken or Just Bruised? Kelly also said Precision had $108 million in cash as of Sept. 30 and recently raised $125 million, taking its cash balance above $200 million. He said the company's cash runway extends into the fourth quarter of 2029. Hepatitis B program moves toward Phase II Gorsuch said 25 patients had received PBGENE-HBV in the repeat-dose Phase I study, with 59 administrations across the group. The company views pgRNA as a primary biomarker for the treatment's effect on cccDNA, the hepatitis B viral material it is designed to eliminate. Gorsuch also said the first e-antigen-positive patient treated in the study had a 3.7-log reduction in pgRNA to undetectable levels at the 0.4 mg/kg dose selected for the next phase. Despite the encouraging biomarker results, Gorsuch said the remaining question is whether the treatment has eliminated enough cccDNA to produce a viral cure. The Phase II study is intended to answer that question. The monotherapy arm will test for viral cure, defined in the discussion as undetectable HBV DNA after treatment is stopped; the combination arm will assess functional cure. Gorsuch said the company sees a potential benefit from reducing viral burden before administering bepirovirsen. Patients in the combination arm will need to meet bepirovirsen eligibility criteria, Gorsuch said. Kelly said Precision had not yet discussed a partnership with GSK but was prepared to purchase bepirovirsen for the study. For patients stopping nucleoside therapy, Gorsuch said normal liver enzymes and fully suppressed HBV DNA are baseline safety considerations. She said regulatory guidance calls for six months off nucleoside treatment to demonstrate an approvable endpoint. Kelly said any withdrawal of therapy in Phase I would be handled case by case, with the larger Phase II study expected to provide more consistent data. Duchenne study awaits biopsy results Precision's Duchenne muscular dystrophy program uses its ARCUS gene-editing technology to remove a region of the dystrophin gene and aims to restore a near full-length dystrophin protein. Gorsuch said the targeted region is mutated in up to 60% of children with the disease. The first patient in the Phase I/II FUNCTION-DMD study had no serious adverse events or adverse events of special interest, Gorsuch said. An independent data safety monitoring board reviewed results through eight weeks after treatment, saw no concerning safety signals and endorsed completing dosing of the first part of the study, she said. Kelly said three-month biopsy data for approximately the first three patients could be available around the second quarter of 2027. The second patient had been enrolled and the third was being screened, he said. Gorsuch said the company believes dystrophin expression above 5% could be therapeutically meaningful, but emphasized that any protein increase must ultimately be linked to functional benefit. Kelly said the first patient's 12-month biopsy data could arrive in the fall of 2027. Gorsuch said the 12-month point would also be more appropriate than three months for beginning to assess functional improvements. About Precision BioSciences (NASDAQ:DTIL) Precision BioSciences is a biotechnology company developing gene-editing therapies using its proprietary ARCUS platform. The platform is designed to make targeted changes to DNA and is being applied to investigational treatments for genetic and infectious diseases. The company's programs include PBGENE-HBV, an investigational therapy designed to target hepatitis B virus DNA, and PBGENE-DMD, a gene-editing program for Duchenne muscular dystrophy. These candidates remain in development and are not approved treatments. news.source_body_en: Precision BioSciences is progressing its Hepatitis B treatment program into Phase II trials, aiming to evaluate the treatment alone and in combination with bepirovirsen, with initial data expected in the second half of 2027. The company reported that the first patient in the Phase I study experienced no serious adverse events, and the safety board has endorsed continued dosing. The Phase II trial involves 25 patients who received PBGENE-HBV in Phase I, with 59 administrations overall. Following a $125 million raise, the company has over $200 million in cash, extending its financial runway to the fourth quarter of 2029. The evidence does not specify any risk level or unresolved issues, indicating that the trial is currently on track with no major concerns raised.

news.content_title: Newborn vaccination rates for hepatitis B drop sharply
news.content: A worker applies an adhesive bandage to a child at a vaccination clinic in Minneapolis' Corcoran Park in August 2023. A new study found the nationwide percentage of newborns receiving the hepatitis B vaccination has declined sharply since 2023. (Photo courtesy of the City of Minneapolis) The percentage of newborns receiving the hepatitis B vaccine has declined sharply in recent years, falling to 65.6% in June 2026 from 79.8% in 2022, according to a new study published Nov. 24 in the New England Journal of Medicine. The authors of the peer-reviewed study looked at health records from more than 1.3 million infants and found that the percentage of babies receiving the hepatitis B vaccination within one day of birth began declining around 2023. The study also found that fewer mothers testing positive for hepatitis B got the vaccine for their babies, from around 98% of those infants in 2025 to around 94% in 2026. A panel of federal vaccine advisers, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, voted in December 2025 to end the longtime recommendation for infants to receive the hepatitis B vaccination at birth even if the mom tested negative. That decision is on hold pending legal challenges. The study was based on data from Truveta, a health data and analytics company owned and governed by 30 health systems across the nation. In explaining the December change, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said screening of pregnant women is highly reliable and can spot disease early. But Nina Masters, an author of the new study and a principal applied research scientist at Truveta specializing in infectious disease and maternal health, told Stateline that "not every mother is tested during pregnancy, and not every person who gets tested has a known status." "And screening is imperfect," she said. "This birth dose has been a universal recommendation to be a safety net to catch those kids that might fall through the cracks, and what we're seeing here is that that safety net is kind of falling apart." Hepatitis B is a contagious liver infection that can cause symptoms of fatigue, loss of appetite and jaundice, and potentially lead to cancer. But it can be prevented through a vaccination. The virus can be passed down from an infected mother to a baby, so since 1991 , the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has recommended that all newborns receive the hepatitis B vaccination within a day after birth to prevent early infections, especially when mothers test positive. A 2023 study by CDC researchers found that between 1990 and 2019, with the recommendation for newborn vaccination, there was a 99% decline in reported cases of acute hepatitis B among people younger than 19 years old. It's official: Measles is endemic again in the US But amid growing vaccination skepticism, the new study found that fewer babies are getting the shot. The shift began a few years before vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. became secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services in February 2025. Researchers noted the decline in vaccination rates for hepatitis B comes as the federal government and many conservative states walk back vaccine mandates for children. Just this month, the United States lost its status as a country that had eliminated measles, as the transmission of measles has risen in the last year. Children are particularly susceptible to the disease. "When messaging gets confusing and there's different recommendations coming from different medical bodies and different kinds of assessments of vaccine safety that are being publicized, I think it can become scary and hard to make the right choice," Masters said. "And I think that's what we're seeing is just extreme confusion as a result of the level of misinformation and changing recommendations around pediatric vaccines." Stateline reporter Shalina Chatlani can be reached at schatlani@stateline.org . analysis.time: The study's findings were reported in June 2026, with the decline in vaccination rates noted since 2023. The CDC's decision to change the recommendation was made in December 2025, and the study's publication date is November 24, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The decline in newborn vaccination rates for hepatitis B was observed nationwide in the United States, affecting infants and mothers, particularly those in conservative states and pregnant women.
analysis.event: A new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine on November 24, 2026, found that the percentage of newborns receiving the hepatitis B vaccine has dropped sharply from 79.8% in 2022 to 65.6% in June 2026. The CDC also changed its recommendation in December 2025, ending the universal recommendation for hepatitis B vaccination at birth, even for infants of mothers who tested negative.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study analyzed data from over 1.3 million infants and found a decline in vaccination rates, with fewer mothers testing positive for hepatitis B receiving the vaccine for their babies. The CDC's decision to revise the recommendation is on hold due to legal challenges. The decline in vaccination rates could increase the risk of hepatitis B transmission from mothers to infants, potentially leading to chronic infections and associated complications like cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study's authors and the CDC acknowledge that screening for hepatitis B during pregnancy is not perfect and that the birth dose served as a safety net. The study's findings are based on health records and data from Truveta, a health data analytics company, and are subject to further investigation and clarification.

analysis.brief_en: A new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine on November 24, 2026, reveals a sharp decline in newborn hepatitis B vaccination rates in the United States, dropping from 79.8% in 2022 to 65.6% in June 2026. The decline is attributed to a shift in federal vaccine recommendations, with the CDC ending its universal recommendation for hepatitis B vaccination at birth in December 2025, even for infants of mothers who tested negative. This decision is on hold due to legal challenges. The study, based on health records from over 1.3 million infants, highlights that fewer mothers testing positive for hepatitis B are receiving the vaccine for their babies, from around 98% in 2025 to 94% in 2026. The CDC acknowledges that screening during pregnancy is not perfect, and the birth dose has served as a safety net to prevent early infections. The decline in vaccination rates raises concerns about increased transmission risks from infected mothers to infants, potentially leading to chronic infections and associated complications like cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. The study's authors emphasize the importance of maintaining vaccination rates to prevent these outcomes, especially in the context of growing vaccine skepticism and the rollback of mandates in some states.

analysis_zh.location_and_population: 在美国全国范围内,新生儿乙型肝炎 疫苗接种 率下降,影响到婴儿和母亲,特别是保守州的婴儿和母亲以及孕妇。
analysis_zh.event: 2026 年 11 月 24 日发表在《新英格兰医学杂志》上的一项新研究发现,新生儿感染乙型肝炎 疫苗 的比例已从 2022 年的 79.8% 急剧下降至 2026 年 6 月的 65.6%。CDC 还在 2025 年 12 月更改了建议,终止了出生时普遍建议感染乙型肝炎 疫苗,即使对于接受过检测的母亲的婴儿也是如此。消极的。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: The study analyzed data from over 1.3 million infants and found a decline in vaccination rates, with fewer mothers testing positive for hepatitis B receiving the vaccine for their babies. The CDC's decision to revise the recommendation is on hold due to legal challenges. The decline in vaccination rates could increase the risk of hepatitis B transmission from mothers to infants, potentially leading to chronic infections and associated complications like cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 该研究的作者和疾病预防控制中心承认,怀孕期间的乙型肝炎筛查并不完美,出生剂量只是一个安全网。该研究的结果基于健康记录和健康数据分析公司 Truveta 的数据,并有待进一步调查和澄清。

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 27, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Dual Hepatitis B and HIV Functional Cure Requires Dedicated Coinfected Clinical Trials by November 26, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Dual Hepatitis B and HIV Functional Cure Requires Dedicated Coinfected Clinical Trials Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A comprehensive narrative review published in Infectious Diseases and Therapy critically evaluates the scientific feasibility of achieving a dual functional cure in patients with concurrent hepatitis B virus and HIV-1 infections. Co-infection constitutes a severe global syndemic affecting approximately 3.4 million people worldwide, in which each pathogen exacerbates the clinical course and morbidity of the other. Although combination antiretroviral therapy suppresses viral replication for both pathogens, it requires lifelong adherence and rarely eliminates either infection. A functional cure is defined in hepatitis B as sustained seroclearance of hepatitis B surface antigen for at least twenty-four weeks alongside undetectable viral DNA, and in HIV-1 as durable treatment-free virological control. The primary obstacle remains the persistence of cellular viral reservoirs, specifically covalently closed circular DNA for hepatitis B and integrated proviral DNA for HIV-1. The global distribution of dual infection is highly uneven, shaped by shared transmission routes including sexual contact, parenteral exposure, and perinatal transmission. At the close of 2024, approximately 40.8 million individuals were living with HIV-1 globally, among whom pooled prevalence of hepatitis B surface antigen positivity was 8.4 percent, representing roughly 3.4 million coinfected individuals. Regional pooled prevalence reaches 12.4 percent in West and Central Africa and 9.8 percent across the Asia-Pacific region, compared to 5.1 percent in Latin America and 6.0 percent in Western Europe and North America. Independent cohort studies in Nigeria, Ghana, and Ethiopia documented coinfection rates between 10 and 15 percent, while China national treatment registry data identified coinfection in 8.7 percent of 33,861 patients. Key documented risk factors include male sex, detention, higher HIV load, lower CD4 cell counts, and lack of hepatitis B vaccination. The biological interaction between the two viruses is bidirectional and deleterious rather than a simple co-occurrence. HIV-1 infection causes severe CD4 T-cell depletion and chronic immune activation, upregulating programmed death-1 and programmed death ligand-1 pathways that induce profound T-cell exhaustion. This immunosuppressive environment impairs essential hepatitis B immune clearance mechanisms normally mediated by cytotoxic CD8 T cells, natural killer cells, neutralizing antibodies, and interferon signaling pathways. Conversely, hepatitis B infection alters the clinical trajectory of HIV-1. Coinfected patients present with lower baseline CD4 counts and elevated transaminases upon starting antiretroviral therapy, and experience slower early CD4 recovery over the initial four years. Furthermore, molecular studies demonstrate that the hepatitis B virus X protein directly enhances HIV-1 long terminal repeat transcription by interacting with host CCAAT/enhancer binding proteins and regulatory elements, confirming that hepatitis B actively modulates HIV-1 persistence. Anatomically, the human liver serves as a shared sanctuary harboring viral reservoirs for both pathogens. Hepatitis B virus establishes stable intranuclear covalently closed circular DNA within hepatocytes, while HIV-1 infects hepatocytes, resident Kupffer cells, and liver-infiltrating CD4 T cells, persisting even throughout suppressive antiretroviral therapy. Microbial translocation across compromised intestinal mucosa releases lipopolysaccharide and soluble CD14 into circulation, driving intrahepatic expression of inflammatory chemokines like CXCL10 and CCL2. Elevated intrahepatic CXCL10 strongly correlates with accelerated liver fibrosis in coinfected cohorts. Concurrently, HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein gp120 binds chemokine receptor CCR5 on hepatic stellate cells to promote profibrogenic signaling, while enhanced hypoxia-inducible factor-1 alpha and transforming growth factor-beta-1 activity exacerbates collagen accumulation. Because hepatic HIV persistence maintains localized immune activation, curative regimens must target both viral reservoirs within hepatic tissue rather than focusing exclusively on peripheral blood compartments. This severe pathogenic interplay translates into accelerated liver disease progression and heightened oncological vulnerability. Clinical data from a Spanish cohort showed that 20 to 25 percent of men living with HIV-1 developed chronic hepatitis B following acute infection, compared to only 5 percent among immunocompetent adults. Hepatocellular carcinoma incidence reaches 1.8 cases per 1,000 person-years in North American coinfection cohorts and 1.7 cases in Swiss studies. Major independent risk factors for liver cancer include age over forty years, hepatitis C coinfection, alcohol use, HIV viremia exceeding 500 copies per milliliter, hepatitis B viral loads above 200 international units per milliliter, low CD4 counts, and pre-existing cirrhosis. Although tenofovir-containing regimens significantly reduce hepatocellular carcinoma incidence, increasing patient longevity elevates the lifetime risk of cirrhosis. Furthermore, a meta-analysis encompassing 12,382 participants revealed that hepatitis B coinfection significantly increases overall all-cause mortality among individuals receiving antiretroviral therapy. In chronic hepatitis B monoinfection, curative benchmarks highlight the contrast between suppressive nucleoside analogs and immunomodulatory interventions. Approved oral agents like entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, and tenofovir alafenamide clear circulating viral DNA in over 90 percent of patients within one year, yet achieve surface antigen seroclearance in only about 1 percent. By comparison, pegylated interferon-alpha strategies achieve surface antigen loss rates ranging from 3 to 65 percent depending on baseline criteria. In the OSST trial, switching from entecavir to pegylated interferon-alpha yielded 8.5 percent overall antigen seroclearance, rising to 22.2 percent in patients with antigen levels below 1,500 international units per milliliter and 77.8 percent below 200 international units. The NEW SWITCH trial recorded 14.4 percent and 20.7 percent seroclearance at 48 and 96 weeks, while the Everest study involving 15,896 patients achieved 26.4 percent loss. Novel agents such as bepirovirsen have also demonstrated meaningful functional cure outcomes. In HIV-1 research, curative strategies distinguish complete sterilizing cure from functional remission maintaining viremia below 50 copies per milliliter without antiretroviral therapy. Spontaneous control occurs in fewer than 1 percent of infected individuals, recognized as elite controllers who possess protective HLA class I alleles and effective immune responses. However, long-term remission in the Geneva patient transplanted with wild-type CCR5 cells and the second Berlin patient receiving heterozygous donor cells indicates that complete coreceptor absence is not strictly mandatory. Given the extreme risks of transplantation, scalable approaches focus on CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing to disrupt CCR5 or CXCR4 coreceptors, successfully conferring cellular resistance against viral entry in preclinical evaluations. Alternative functional cure pathways for HIV-1 involve latency-targeting interventions, broadly neutralizing antibodies, and immunomodulatory agents. Under the shock-and-kill strategy, latency-reversing agents including histone deacetylase inhibitors like vorinostat, romidepsin, and panobinostat are deployed to reactivate latent proviruses for immune clearance, while block-and-lock approaches utilize Tat inhibitors to silence transcription permanently. Concurrently, infusions of broadly neutralizing antibodies have demonstrated clinical efficacy; the TITAN trial established that 36 percent of participants sustained viral suppression beyond 25 weeks, while triple antibody combinations achieved control in 83 percent for at least 28 weeks. Pegylated interferon-alpha also possesses dual immunomodulatory potential, producing a median viral decline of 0.61 log10 copies per milliliter in HIV monoinfection and reducing CD4-associated viral reservoirs in coinfected patients with hepatitis C. Despite these individual advancements, their efficacy and translational feasibility in simultaneous hepatitis B and HIV coinfection remain essentially untested. Translating single-infection cure models into coinfection encounters both distinct immunological opportunities and severe clinical hazards. Coinfected individuals receiving long-term suppressive tenofovir-based antiretroviral therapy paradoxically achieve surface antigen clearance rates between 7 and 11 percent, exceeding 10 percent in select cohorts, well above the 1 percent annual rate seen in hepatitis B monoinfection. This phenomenon reflects immune reconstitution, where restoring CD4 counts disrupts pre-existing hepatitis B immune tolerance and provokes hepatic flares that frequently precede antigen loss. However, these hepatic flares pose severe risks of acute decompensation and fatal liver injury. Furthermore, end point assessment introduces a major ethical barrier: while hepatitis B functional cure can be confirmed on active therapy, establishing an HIV functional cure requires an analytical treatment interruption. In coinfected patients, interrupting antiretroviral therapy risks aggressive hepatitis B viral rebound, catastrophic hepatitis flares, and liver failure, and no established protocol currently exists for safe interruption. To navigate these challenges, the authors proposed a four-phase sequential framework as a hypothesis-generating model. Phase one establishes deep dual suppression through at least four to five years of continuous tenofovir-based therapy, which lowers hepatic inflammation, prevents fibrosis progression, and provides an immunological baseline without treatment interruption. Phase two applies retrospective criteria to select optimal candidates, prioritizing patients with surface antigen levels below 1,500 international units per milliliter, favorable genotypes like genotype B, CD4 counts above 350 cells per cubic millimeter, and previous immune flares. Phase three investigates combination immunotherapy by adding pegylated interferon-alpha for 24 to 48 weeks, potentially alongside checkpoint inhibitors, Toll-like receptor 8 agonists, or latency-reversing agents under strict safety monitoring. Phase four involves consolidation, flare monitoring, and hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance, restricting analytical treatment interruption exclusively to clinical trials with rigorous rescue protocols. Advancing this conceptual framework requires dedicated clinical trials and validated biomarkers specifically evaluated in coinfected populations. Early-phase trial designs such as AIDS Clinical Trials Group A5394 illustrate the meticulous safety protocols and biomarker-driven endpoints required for evaluating combination immunotherapies. In accordance with 2025 European Association for the Study of the Liver guidance, clinical studies must evaluate emerging hepatitis B biomarkers, including quantitative surface antigen, hepatitis B core-related antigen, and circulating viral RNA, in parallel with assays quantifying intact HIV reservoirs. Furthermore, single-cell multiomics technologies are needed to simultaneously track virus-specific T-cell responses within the same coinfected individuals, while genotype-guided strategies must address differences across viral lineages. Because historical clinical trials routinely excluded coinfected individuals due to toxicity concerns, the authors conclude that close collaboration between hepatology and HIV research communities is essential to replace theoretical extrapolations with robust clinical evidence. supplementary_news.content: LOADING ERROR LOADING Vaccination rates in children and babies are dropping across the United States. This is made clear by current measles outbreaks in states such as Pennsylvania, New York, Wisconsin and more. Now new research , published in the New England Journal of Medicine Evidence, shows that parents are not only opting their babies out of the measles vaccine, but also the hepatitis B vaccine. The study was conducted by researchers from Callen-Lorde Community Health Center in New York and Truveta, a healthcare data company. Researchers analyzed the medical records of more than 1.3 million babies and found that as of June 2026, 65.6% of newborn babies were vaccinated against hepatitis B in their first 24 hours of life, down from 80% in 2022. While the drop in hepatitis B vaccination rates started in 2023, the continuing decline comes at a time when Trump-era federal vaccine advisers voted to remove the hepatitis B vaccine from the childhood vaccine schedule. (The move is currently blocked by an American Academy of Pediatrics lawsuit , so the hepatitis B shot still remains part of the schedule.) “I find it unfortunate that vaccination rates are declining, because this inevitably means that rates of hepatitis B infection will ultimately rise, and lives will be permanently affected,” said Dr. Leslie Treece , a pediatrician in Tennessee. Treece is not involved with this study. “Prior to 1991, we used to recommend vaccination only to ‘high risk’ groups. In spite of this, there were still about 24,000 cases per year of hepatitis B infection in infants [in the U.S.],” Treece said. “After adopting universal newborn vaccination, the case number dropped dramatically to a few hundred or less cases in the US per year.” Hepatitis B can be lifelong and chronic, and can lead to liver cancer and liver failure. “With hepatitis B, this is especially worrisome because it is a lifelong, chronic disease with no cure, leading to liver failure and liver cancer later in life,” said Dr. Zhen Chan , a pediatrician at Zarminali Pediatrics in Washington, D.C. Chan was not involved with this study. “Both of these diseases can lead to early death,” Chan added. Hepatitis B is not always lifelong and chronic, but it is more likely to be the earlier someone is infected. This vaccine is given to newborns because transmission during birth ― or within the first 24 hours of life from an infected mother ― carries the highest risk of chronic hepatitis B infection and later risk of cancer and liver disease, explained Dr. Alexandra Yonts , a pediatric infectious diseases specialist at Children’s National in Washington, D.C. Yonts is not involved with this study. “About 1 in 4 children with lifelong infection eventually die of cirrhosis or liver cancer if untreated. The longer a baby is left unvaccinated, the higher the chance of getting infected,” Chan said. Sollina Images via Getty Images Hepatitis B vaccination rates are declining in newborns in the United States. Hepatitis B is rare; it’s estimated that 640,000 adults have chronic hepatitis B, but that further points to the power of vaccination. “Many families will question how their baby would even get hepatitis B when the rates are so low. I usually explain that rates are low because of the vaccine itself, and the lower the vaccination rates in the community, the greater the risk of getting the disease,” Chan said. “The safety data supports giving the hepatitis B vaccine at such an early age. Completing the full series gives a baby about a 98% level protection against the disease,” Chan added. Not only does the vaccine prevent babies from infection when they’re young, but it goes on protect against hepatitis B infection when they reach adulthood, said Dr. Rick Malley , a senior physician in pediatrics, division of infectious diseases at Boston Children’s Hospital. Malley is not involved with this study. “The idea of preventive vaccination for diseases that the individual might really only encounter much later in life is one of the great successes of hepatitis B vaccination,” Malley said. “By immunizing children early, we were really preventing ... transmission perinatally, and also providing protection later in life.” The consequences of a decline in hepatitis B vaccination won’t be seen for some time. “There are all these understandable instances of confusion that people might have when they hear their healthcare provider tell them one thing, and then they go on the internet, or they get exposed to some video that tells them exactly the opposite,” said Malley. It’s not surprising that people pause the recommended vaccine schedule when they see conflicting messaging online, he noted. “Unfortunately, we know that when that happens, the likelihood that an individual will get a vaccine-preventable disease increases significantly,” Malley said. The current measles outbreaks throughout the U.S. are just one example of this, and the now decline in hepatitis B vaccination is another, he added. “I think now with hepatitis B, the consequences of of these drops in vaccinations ... may not be observed quite as quickly as we, unfortunately, are seeing with the measles outbreaks,” Malley said. “So, that is also confusing in a way because the consequences of this may not be seen for a while.” “And I think, broadly, it also points to another bit of a problem in the field of vaccines, which is that ... vaccines are really victims of their own success,” he said. Most people don’t know someone who had polio. Most people had not heard about measles until the current outbreak in the U.S. “Trying to convince the public that the reason they don’t know about these terrifying diseases is precisely because of vaccination is a bit of a hurdle,” he said. In the end, “the benefits of preventing chronic Hep B infection and complications of liver disease and liver cancer far outweigh any minor risks ... of vaccination,” Yonts said, adding that there are no major adverse effects or side effects of the vaccine. “Giving this vaccine to every baby ... is the most equitable and responsible thing we can do for our population,” Yonts added. “We shouldn’t make babies (and the future of our country) pay the price of failings of our healthcare for pregnant women.” | Submit a tip

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 27, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology One-Tube Assay Delivers Rapid Visual Detection of Hepatitis B Virus RNA by November 26, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 One-Tube Assay Delivers Rapid Visual Detection of Hepatitis B Virus RNA Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Researchers have developed a novel diagnostic platform, termed One-Tube-PfAgo-HBV-RNA, that provides ultrasensitive, specific, and visual identification of hepatitis B virus RNA. The molecular approach seamlessly combines reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification with Pyrococcus furiosus Argonaute-mediated identification inside a custom-engineered sealed tube. Hepatitis B virus infection remains a pressing global health concern requiring reliable diagnostic strategies. Circulating hepatitis B virus RNA has been proposed as a valuable surrogate biomarker that directly reflects the transcriptional activity of covalently closed circular DNA within virus-infected hepatocytes. By mirroring intrahepatic covalently closed circular DNA activity, measuring circulating viral RNA aids clinicians in assessing therapeutic efficacy and evaluating antiviral treatment response in infected individuals. To establish the One-Tube-PfAgo-HBV-RNA detection system, the investigators designed specific loop-mediated isothermal amplification primers and 5′-phosphorylated guide DNAs targeting hepatitis B virus RNA. The research team systematically evaluated and optimized critical diagnostic parameters governing the performance of the molecular assay. These optimization procedures established the precise reaction temperature required for reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification. Additionally, the investigators systematically calibrated the reaction duration necessary for Pyrococcus furiosus Argonaute-mediated cleavage to ensure reliable target recognition and enzymatic activity. Analytical validation demonstrated that the One-Tube-PfAgo-HBV-RNA assay achieved an ultrasensitive limit of detection of five copies per reaction. Furthermore, analytical specificity testing showed that the platform displayed no cross-reactivity against other microbial species, confirming that the designed primers and guide DNAs selectively identify hepatitis B virus RNA without generating false-positive background results. The entire diagnostic workflow was successfully completed within ninety minutes from initial processing to visual result interpretation. This timeline comprises approximately forty-five minutes for hepatitis B virus RNA preparation, thirty minutes of reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification, ten minutes for Pyrococcus furiosus Argonaute-mediated cleavage, and less than two minutes for visual readout on the gold nanoparticle-based lateral flow biosensor. The clinical feasibility of the diagnostic platform was assessed through serum specimens obtained from chronic hepatitis B patients. When tested on these clinical serum samples, the One-Tube-PfAgo-HBV-RNA assay demonstrated one hundred percent concordance with the standard reference method, quantitative real-time PCR for hepatitis B virus RNA, confirming its clinical diagnostic reliability. The authors concluded that these preliminary results demonstrate considerable promise for the accurate and convenient monitoring of chronic hepatitis B infections. Furthermore, the novel closed-tube platform establishes an important technical foundation for developing point-of-care molecular diagnostics targeting other infectious diseases, particularly for healthcare settings in resource-limited regions.
